Coroplast yard signs and lawn signs: sizes, prices and rules

Yard signs are one of the cheapest ways to get your name in front of a neighbourhood. Here’s how to choose the right type and size, design one that reads from a moving car, and stay on the right side of local sign rules.

By the Satin Graphic teamUpdated October 10, 2026
On this pageCoroplast or poly bag?Prices at our shopSize, sides and stakesDesign that reads from a moving carReal estate signsRules to check before you stake a signMaking signs lastQuestionsRelatedYard signsPoly bag lawn signsLarge format printing

Coroplast or poly bag?

There are two common kinds of lawn sign:

Coroplast (corrugated plastic) yard signPoly bag lawn sign
What it isRigid fluted plastic board, printed in full colourPrinted plastic sleeve that slides over a wire frame
LookFull colour, photos and gradientsOne to three spot colours
DurabilityRated for 2–3 years outdoors; reusableShort-term; best for single campaigns
Sizes at our shop18 × 24 in or 24 × 36 in24 × 20 in or 32 × 20 in
Best forContractors, real estate, events, directional signsLarge runs — elections, community campaigns, promotions

Coroplast is the workhorse: full-colour printing, stiff enough to stay readable in wind, and reusable for job after job. Poly bag signs are the budget option when you need hundreds of identical signs for a short period and a simple one- to three-colour design is enough.

Prices at our shop

From our online configurators, before tax:

  • Coroplast yard signs (18 × 24 in, single-sided): $19.99 for one sign, dropping to $14.56 each from 10 and $11.20 each from 25. The 24 × 36 in size adds $9 per sign, double-sided printing $4, and an H-stake $2.
  • Poly bag lawn signs (24 × 20 in, one colour): about $7 each for 50, $4.41 each for 100 and $3.92 each for 1,000.

There’s no minimum on coroplast signs — one is fine. See yard signs and poly bag lawn signs for the live calculators.

Size, sides and stakes

18 × 24 in is the standard lawn sign — big enough to read from the street in a residential neighbourhood, small enough to carry a stack in a car. 24 × 36 in reads from further away and suits corner lots, wider roads, construction sites and open houses.

Double-sided printing is worth it whenever the sign stands perpendicular to the road, so drivers see it in both directions. For a sign facing the street flat against a fence, single-sided is enough.

H-stakes (wire stakes that slide into the flutes of the coroplast) are the standard way to mount a yard sign in grass. If you’re mounting to a fence, wall or post instead, skip the stakes and ask about grommets or screws.

Design that reads from a moving car

A yard sign is usually seen for two or three seconds from a car 10 to 20 metres away. Design accordingly:

  • Five to seven words maximum — for example, “Kitchen renovation by [Your Company]” plus a phone number or short web address.
  • One contact method, printed as large as possible. A short, memorable website often works better than a phone number for people who see it while driving.
  • Thick, simple fonts and strong contrast: dark on light or light on dark. Avoid thin scripts and light colours on white.
  • Big logo, small decoration. Photos rarely read at a distance on a sign this size.
  • QR codes only make sense for people on foot — useful for real estate and open houses, less so for signs aimed at traffic.

Artwork should be built at final size at 100–150 DPI, with a 0.25 in bleed for rigid signs. For poly bag signs, vector artwork in one to three solid spot colours works best. If you need help, add design to your order.

Real estate signs

Agents use coroplast for open-house and directional signs and often use a 24 × 36 in sign with a rider or a post-mounted panel for listings. A few practical tips:

  • Keep the brokerage branding consistent with your board’s and brokerage’s requirements — check your brokerage’s sign policy before printing.
  • Directional arrows should be double-sided and huge; the arrow is the message.
  • Order a few spares; directional signs disappear.

Rules to check before you stake a sign

Where you can put a temporary sign is set by municipal sign by-laws, which differ between Vaughan, Toronto, Markham, Mississauga, Brampton and every other GTA municipality. Common themes:

  • Private property: you generally need the owner’s permission, and some by-laws limit size, number and how long a temporary sign can stay up.
  • Public property: placing signs on boulevards, medians, road allowances, parks and utility poles is often restricted or prohibited, and municipalities can remove signs placed there.
  • Election signs follow separate rules on when they can go up and must come down, set by each municipality for municipal elections and also affected by provincial and federal election rules.
  • Sight lines: never place a sign where it blocks drivers’ view at corners or driveways.

This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current sign by-law on your city’s website or call 311 (where available) before a campaign.

Making signs last

Coroplast and the latex inks we print with are rated for 2–3 years outdoors, but most signs are retired long before they fade because they get bent, lost or outdated. Store reusable signs flat and dry, pull stakes straight up to avoid splitting the flutes, and design “evergreen” job-site signs without dates or prices so you can reuse them for years.

Questions

What is the standard yard sign size?
18 × 24 inches. Choose 24 × 36 inches for corner lots, busier roads or when you need to be read from further away.
How long do coroplast signs last outside?
Printed coroplast signs are rated for about 2–3 years outdoors. Most are retired earlier because they get bent or the message changes.
How much do yard signs cost?
At our shop, an 18 × 24 in single-sided coroplast sign is $19.99 for one, falling to $11.20 each from 25 signs, before tax. Poly bag lawn signs start around $3.92 each in quantities of 1,000.
Can I put a sign on the boulevard in front of my business?
Often not without permission. Boulevards and road allowances are usually public property and are covered by municipal sign by-laws. Check with your city before placing a sign there.
Should I choose single- or double-sided?
Double-sided if the sign stands perpendicular to the road so drivers see it from both directions; single-sided if it faces the street flat.
